**An Editable Blockchain Based Framework for Secure Student Evaluation**

 Soumyadip Chowdhury1, Souvik Basu2, Sipra Das Bit1

1 Indian Institute of Engineering Science and Technology, Shibpur, India  
2 Heritage Institute of Technology, Kolkata, India

**Abstract.** In the post COVID 19 pandemic era, universities have shifted to digital platforms for imparting education and student evaluation. Digital evaluation typically involves database management systems for keeping the students’ records, which are vulnerable to a single point of failure, security breaches, and other difficulties of a centralized system. Researchers have proposed the usage of blockchain technology to alleviate these challenges, as blocks in a blockchain are distributed among numerous network nodes and are also tamperproof, hence highly secure. However, this immutability of blockchain technology restricts the possibility of modifying a student's marks, stored in a block, even for legitimate reasons. Such a scenario calls for creating an editable blockchain for storing students’ marks. Keeping this requirement in mind, in this paper, we propose an editable blockchain based framework for student evaluation to enable editing of the records in a block for legitimate reasons while making the evaluation process confidential, accurate, and transparent. The framework, implemented on the Ethereum platform, uses open-source libraries and smart contracts written in Solidity, generates marks, and successfully stores them into the blocks of a blockchain as transactions. The framework performs well in terms of blockchain overhead metrics like execution cost, gas consumption, and transaction cost for contract deployment, with a varying number of students and authority levels. In particular, there is only 5% – 10% average increase in the aforementioned overheads with an increasing number of students from 200 to 500\.

            **Keywords:** University education system; Student evaluation; Blockchain; Smart Contract; Transaction

**1\. Introduction** 

A university education system consists of different functional modules; one of the most important modules is students’ evaluation and assessment. Assessment techniques can be traditional pen and paper-based examinations or a digital evaluation system. Typically, after evaluation by the examiner, the obtained marks are reviewed by the scrutinizer, Head Examiner, Tabulator, and Controller of Examination one by one. At each stage, if there is any need for rectification/correction, it is done by the respective authority concerned. If the assessment technique is a traditional pen and paper based examination, digital record keeping may be done partially (e.g., Tabulator, Controller of Examinations) in an isolated manner.

In spite of the fact that many institutions all over the world prefer traditional systems till today, during the recent COVID-19 pandemic, each institution was compelled to conduct digital assessment. Since the present era is transforming digitally, a smart education system is highly preferred. For a digital evaluation system \[3\], a university typically uses database management systems for keeping the students’ records. However, usage of such a system is a centralized procedure and often leads to a single point of failure. Moreover, it may be under a security threat from unauthorized user(s).   
Researchers have proposed the usage of blockchain technology to alleviate these challenges \[7\], as blockchain allows the data stored in the database to be distributed among numerous network nodes at several places \[1 \- 11\]. Also, the blocks in a blockchain are tamperproof and hence highly secure \[11\]. The usage of blockchain for storing students’ marks, thus becomes highly imperative. In light of the above discussion, in the evaluation workflow, all personnel may be considered as the nodes of the blockchain. If the examiner keeps the marks in his/her blocks of the blockchain \[10\], all other nodes will be able to see the blocks and keep that too because of the flooding transmission. Now, for evaluation purposes, after completion of the examiner’s entry, if the scrutinizer tries to rectify any marks, s/he won’t be able to do so because other nodes will prevent the rectification due to the immutability characteristic of blockchain. This immutability of blockchain technology restricts the possibility of modifying a student's marks even for legitimate reasons. Although it is an essential part of the evaluation process to rectify marks as and when required by the authorized personnel. Such a scenario calls for creating an editable blockchain \[6\] for storing students’ marks. Keeping this requirement in mind, in this paper, we propose an editable blockchain based framework for student evaluation to enable editing of the records in a block for legitimate reasons while making the evaluation process confidential, accurate, and transparent. This ultimately makes the process tamperproof yet editable  
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarizes a review of existing literature on the usage of blockchain in education, as well as a student evaluation system. Section 3 describes the proposed methodology, and Section 4 elucidates the practical implementation of the proposed methodology. The paper concludes in Section 5 with a direction towards future research.

**2\. Literature Review** 

There has been substantial research on the applications of blockchain technology for executing different educational activities \[8\], such as student evaluation, result generation, student records management, teacher performance evaluation, etc.   
Kaur et al. in \[2\] create a blockchain based framework for educators (essentially the teachers), which helps with their future employability. The work develops a supervisory entity (software module) that uploads the feedback and performance of educators to the blockchain ledger through a smart contract. Sharma et al. in \[4\] attempt to understand blockchain technology and its application in educational record keeping. Ocheja et al. in \[5\] present a unique bibliometric and qualitative review on several blockchain technology based education systems. They focus on identifying the key contributors from different demographic areas, the adoption of existing emerging topics, grey areas, and possible areas for innovation. Ouyang et al. in \[12\] adopt the blockchain technology for evaluating modern education. It creates an educational evaluation management mechanism by cooperating with educational institutions and supports the implementation of quality measures and policies. The goal of Alam et al. in \[13\] is to study an educational system that uses blockchain along with the Internet of Things for cryptographically securing records. Authors combine blockchain and IoT to create an efficient online interaction system among students, teachers, employers, developers, facilitators, recruiters, and accreditation organizations. Duan et al. in \[17\] propose a learning outcome based evaluation system using blockchain technology, which uses an automated evaluation software. Turkanovi´c et al. in \[15\] propose EduCTX, a global higher education credit platform which is based on the idea of the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS). Averin et al. in \[16\] describe the model for monitoring student performance in an educational institute. The model handles issuance of diplomas using blockchain technology, its elements and structure, the process of diplomas release, the possibility of further verification of diplomas, and student grades. Samanta et al. in \[17\] analyse the public and private blockchains’ security issues in student evaluation and designed their proposed prototype system to solve them. Taking a heterogeneous data structure, the authors present a case study on a university examination system. Abougalala et al. in \[18\] present a conceptual framework for illustrating the usage of blockchain technology in smart universities to support and ensure a better understanding of the participation of the students with the university.   
The above literature review emphasizes that although considerable works have been done on the usage of blockchain technology in various aspects of an education system \[2, 4, 5, 7, 8\], especially in the domain of student evaluation \[9 \- 13\], however, no such work has so far been done for

* ensuring immutability and transparency at every step of student evaluation    
* allowing editing of marks for legitimate reasons, which is imperative for any evaluation system    
* involving all types of authorized personnel in the blockchain network (e.g., Scrutinizer, Head Examiner, Tabulator, Controller of Examination) in the evaluation system

This motivates us to propose an editable blockchain based framework for student evaluation, which exploits the benefits of using blockchain as well as relaxing the restrictions of such a system. The objectives of the proposed blockchain based framework for student evaluation are as follows:  

* storing students’ marks in a blockchain at each step of evaluation to incorporate immutability    
* Involving all types of authorized personnel in the blockchain network (e.g. Examiner, Scrutinizer, Head Examiner, Tabulator) to bring transparency in the evaluation process    
* enabling the blockchain network to allow editing of the evaluated marks at every steps of evaluation for legitimate reason, which is essential for such a system    
* implementing the student evaluation framework on the Ethereum blockchain platform

**3\. Proposed Methodology**

In this section, we elaborate on the proposed editable blockchain based framework for secure student evaluation. In our proposed framework, we create a separate blockchain for each subject. As mentioned in the Introduction, the stakeholders work at two different levels – the authority level and the user level. The stakeholders at the admin level are examiners, scrutinizers, head examiners, tabulators, and the controller of examinations.   
On the other hand, the user level stakeholders are students, recruiters, and monitoring bodies. We know that blockchain does not allow modification of transactions already deployed in a block, because of its immutability characteristic. However, in a student’s evaluation system, justified modification of the marks is important. If all the authorities enter the same marks of a given subject for any particular student, there is no need for modification. If any of them enter different marks of the subject, it calls for modification ofthe  marks that are already deployed in a block of the blockchain. For this, each of the authorities except the examiner needs to add remarks if the marks awarded by him/her to a particular student vary from the marks awarded by the previous authority levels.   
To make the blockchain editable, the blockchain miners have to fire a query to check whether these modifications are valid or not, by checking the remarks added by an authority level user. Now, one of the shortcomings of blockchain is its inability to process search queries, due to the absence of a data indexing structure \[14\]. On the other hand, a database has a defined indexing structure that is optimized \[14\] for fast query processing. However, the database may be tampered with by malicious users, including the database administrator. Also, the database cannot activate the backup-based recovery scheme without manual intervention when the system fails, causing data loss.   
Thus, in our proposed framework, we use a blockchain based database system that has the combined features of the blockchain and the distributed databases \[19\]. A node in the blockchain network has its own copy of the blockchain data. In the proposed framework, when a miner wants to validate any marks given by an authority level that does not match with marks given by the previous authority levels, it fires a query to the database. If the database has a remark corresponding to changed marks, the miner validates the marks and updates its local copy of the blockchain. This local copy is then propagated in the peer-to-peer network for the necessary global update.   
As per the evaluation workflow, firstly, the examiners evaluate the answer scripts and upload the marks using an online portal dedicated to them. These marks remain temporarily stored in a database until the completion of the entire script’s evaluation. When examiners complete the evaluation of all the scripts, all the marks from that database are uploaded into a block of the blockchain. So, this block becomes the first block, which is termed the Genesis Block. Due to the flooding mechanism of blockchain, all nodes in the peer-to-peer blockchain network get the contents of the first block, having the evaluated marks, which are now ready for scrutiny. Then the scrutinizers review all the evaluated marks from their dedicated online portal, and if there is any discrepancy, the marks are to be rectified with proper justification. At this stage, the marks are again temporarily stored in the database until the completion of the scrutiny. Upon completion of scrutiny, the marks are ready for uploading into the blockchain. Now, if the scrutinizer's marks and examiner’s marks of the current and previous transactions do not match, it is not allowed to be uploaded to the new block.   
However, from the perspective of our student evaluation system, this is one of the most essential requirements. We need to edit an already deployed block so that the marks of a student in the examiner's block and the scrutinizer's block remain the same. As mentioned before, to edit an already deployed block, the blockchain miners have to fire a query to the corresponding database to check whether these modifications are valid or not, based on the remarks provided in the database. After the successful validity checking of the scrutinized marks, miner will upload a new transaction into a block and modify the same to the previous block, i.e., the examiner’s block.   
Then the head examiner will recheck the scrutinized marks from his/her dedicated online portal, and if there is any discrepancy, the marks will be rectified with proper remarks. Same procedure for scrutinized marks rectification will be repeated in this case also, and a new transaction will be uploaded into a block and modified the same to the examiner’s and scrutinizer’s blocks. The same procedure will be repeated for the tabulator and controller of examinations. Thus, our objective of connecting the blockchain with the database to make the blockchain editable for rectification of the marks in a block with legitimate justification is achieved. **4\. Practical Implementation**

In this section, we describe the practical implementation of the methodology pertaining to the proposed blockchain based framework for secure student evaluation on the Ethereum blockchain platform. In particular, we describe the implementation setup, execution procedure, sample execution scenarios, and blockchain overheads. 

**4.1. Implementation Setup** 

The blockchain platform used for implementing the proposed framework is Ethereum running on Truffle v4.5. The rationale behind using Ethereum is that it provides a broader range of validation strategies compared to other blockchain platforms, with the power of smart contracts written through Solidity code. We have used Geth v1.7.0 as a wallet for message transferring. A computer system with an Intel® CoreTM CPU with 2.0 GHz, 8 GB of RAM, and 20 GB of persistent storage has been used to meet the minimum hardware requirements for running Ethereum.

**4.2. Execution Procedure** 

The practical implementation of the proposed framework has the following execution procedure.

*Step 1*: When a user enters his/her details into the marks portal, the user is authenticated. 

*Step 2*: Once authenticated, if a user enters as admin, he/she has to select the exact authority level.   
*Step 2.1*:The Authority must put the exact credentials for further redirection. Credentials, along with the current authority level, are sent to an ExpressJS endpoint. Data collected from the authority is validated with information present in a database created by MongoDB. A flag is sent if validated from ExpressJS. Response of the flag is essential to redirect to the page for selecting the department and course.   
*Step 2.2*: With the selection of department and course, the portal will then require the authority to select the semester for which students’ marks are to be entered.   
*Step 2.3*: With the selection of a semester, a query will be executed to get all the subjects that are provided in that semester, to be displayed for that particular department.   
*Step 2.4*: The Subject should be selected, and the user will be redirected to the page where a list of students of that department is displayed, with provision for entering marks.   
*Step 2.5*: When marks for all students are entered, the data are written onto the database. ExpressJS will be playing the pivotal role of accepting and sending data through endpoints throughout the entire validation, read, write, and update operations between the backend (database- MongoDB) and the frontend (ReactJS). With the data written to the database, write permission will be removed for that authority level of that subject belonging to the semester of a particular department.  
*Step 2.6*: Now the entire list of marks is ready to be uploaded to the blockchain. Smart contracts are executed to check the validity of the marks by firing a query to the database before any transaction is made.   
*Step 2.7*: To fulfil the transaction, some amount of testnetETH is needed in the Metamask wallet. Sepoliatestnet is used for development purposes. The transaction will cost some ETH (inclusive of Gas price).   
*Step 2.8*: After the fulfillment of the transaction, data will be deployed to the blockchain and will be immutable but transparent. 

*Step 3*: Once authenticated, if a user enters as a student, the same procedure of verification of a student will be done on the login page, as in Step 2.1.   
*Step 3.1*: With the selection of the semester, a query will be executed to get all the subjects that are provided in that semester, to be displayed for that particular department.   
*Step 3.2*: With that selection, the student can view the obtained marks in every subject, which will be fetched from the blockchain and presented in a relevant format.

**4.3. Performance Evaluation** 

In this section, we provide a performance evaluation of the proposed editable blockchain-based framework for secure student evaluation. We conduct three sets of experiments for this purpose. We consider three blockchain overhead metrics, such as execution cost, transaction cost, and GAS price \[20\]. The metrics are defined \[19\] below: 

***Execution Cost:*** This represents the amount of gas needed to carry out smart contracts, pertaining to a transaction. The unit is a gas.   
***Transaction Cost:*** This represents the total amount of gas needed during the transaction. Transaction cost includes both execution cost and the transaction's inherent costs. The unit is a gas.   
***GAS Price:*** This is the amount of Ether that is spent on each unit of gas. The unit is wei, where 1 ETH \= 1018 wei.

**4.3.1. Experimental Result on Execution Cost** 

In the first set of experiments, the impact of varying the number of students and authority levels on the execution cost is measured. Figure 2(a) plots the result, which shows that execution cost increases with increasing number of students but remains the same with the increase in the number of authority levels. It is observed that execution cost increases by 97% when the number of students is raised from 100 to 200, whereas execution cost increases by only 26% when the number of students is raised from 200 to 500\. So, only the initial execution cost is increased heavily with the increased number of students. 

![][image3]

**Figure. 2(a)** Effect of no. of students on Execution Cost

**4.3.2. Experimental Result on Transaction Cost** 

In the second set of experiments, the impact of varying the number of students and authority levels on the transaction cost is measured. Figure 2(b) plots the results, which show that transaction cost increases with an increasing number of students but remains the same with the increase in the number of authority levels. It is observed that execution cost increases by 95% when the number of students is raised from 100 to 200, whereas execution cost increases by only 24% when the number of students is raised from 200 to 500\. So, only the initial execution cost is increased significantly with the increased number of students.  
![][image4]  
![][image5]

**Figure. 2(b)** Effect of no. of students on Transaction Cost

**4.3.3. Experimental Result on GAS Price**

In the third set of experiments, the impact of varying numbers of students and authority levels on the transaction cost is measured. Figure 2(c) plots the results, which show that transaction cost increases with increasing number of students but remains the same with the increase in the number of authority levels. It is observed that execution cost increases by 95% when the number of students is raised from 100 to 200, whereas execution cost increases by only 24% when the number of students is raised from 200 to 500\. So, only the initial execution cost is increased significantly with the increased number of students.  
![][image6]  
**Figure. 2(c)** Effect of no. of students on the Gas Price

We observe from the above experiments that execution cost, transaction cost, and gas price are not increasing with increasing authority level from 2 to 5\. The reason is that, in the proposed framework, adding an authority level to the existing ones engages the execution of only one smart contract for uploading updated students’ marks. These updated marks are stored in a new block. Executing only one smart contract does not have any significant effect on the performance metrics. On the contrary, execution cost, transaction cost, and gas price are increasing by 5% to 10%, on average, with an increasing number of students from 200 to 500\. The sharp increase in the blockchain parameters when student number is raised from 100 to 200 may be attributed to the high platform usage beyond a certain instance in time.

**5\. Conclusion and Future Work** 

In this paper, an editable blockchain based framework is proposed for student evaluation to make the evaluation process confidential, accurate, and transparent. The proposed framework allows editing of a block for modification of the records in that particular block with legitimate justification, only to make an ultimately tamperproof yet rational blockchain. The framework, implemented on the Ethereum platform, uses open-source libraries and smart contracts written in Solidity, generates marks, and successfully stores them into the blocks of a blockchain as transactions. Modified transactions are also successfully stored in the blocks. The framework performs well in terms of blockchain overhead metrics like execution cost, gas consumption, and transaction cost for contract deployment, with a varying number of students and authority levels. In particular, there is only 5% – 10% average increase in the aforementioned overheads with an increasing number of students from 200 to 500\. However, this average does not take into consideration the sharp increase from the ‘100 students scenario’ to the ‘200 students scenario’, caused due to high platform usage beyond a certain instance in time. In the future, we aim to use natural language processing tools to analyze these remarks and take necessary decisions to make the proposed framework intelligent and self-adaptive.
